newsitem.title: CANADA: Loewen comfortable with earnings estimates.
newsitem.headline: Loewen comfortable with earnings estimates.

text.p: The Loewen Group Inc is comfortable with analysts' estimates for 1997 earnings per share in the range of US$1.70, chief executive Ray Loewen said in an interview Friday.
"Analysts are projecting in the US$1.70 range for the next year....We are comfortable today with analysts' projections," he said.

So far in 1997, Loewen -- the second biggest operator in its industry in North America after Service Corp -- has signed US$40 million in acquisitions, mainly in small towns, which are the most profitable market for acquirers, he said.

The average return on investment on those deals would be on a par with or slightly higher than the company's historic average of 16 percent in the first year for funeral homes and in the second year for cemeteries, Loewen said.
Loewen did about US$1.4 billion in deals last year, including US$830 million in acquisitions and US$535 million in structured acquisition transactions.
The funeral home and cemetery operator is not due to report fourth-quarter results until early March.

For the first nine months of 1996, it earned US$0.84 a share, and analysts forecast Loewen would earn about US$0.41 a share in the fourth quarter, excluding costs associated with fighting a now abandoned hostile takeover bid by rival Service Corp International. The company said previously said it is comfortable with those fourth-quarter estimates.
Loewen said his company, which has grown rapidly by buying funeral homes and cemeteries in the United States, expected 1997 acquisitions to total US$600 million to US$750 million.
Further structured transactions like those it did with New York merchant bank Blackstone Group last year are not currently envisaged, Loewen said.
Loewen said his company is likely to raise equity and debt within the next year although nothing is imminent.

"We have a healthy balance sheet today. There is no immediate interest or need in raising equity. But some time in the next year I'm sure we will," he said. "Our need for capital is such, some time in the next year, we will need to do another bond."

Loewen said he was confident the company was back to its traditional earnings per share growth rate, which averaged 27 percent a year before the company found itself on the brink of bankruptcy due to a damage award last January and then fighting a hostile takeover bid from Service by September.
The company's stock price, currently around US$36, is well below Service's US$43 a share offer, which it withdrew this month.

But Loewen predicted that when investors see evidence of the company's strong growth, its share price will recover. He said it historically traded around 25 to 30 times projected earnings which would mean about US$51 currently.
"I think we need to get through year-end and first quarter (earnings reports) and our shareholders will have the comfort they need," Loewen said.
